answer: DATA-GROUNDED HYPOTHESIS: The premise of a Black "advantage" in BA/degree completion is NOT supported by this NLSY79 sample — Black respondents show the LOWEST educational attainment on every measure (mean grade completed 9.8 vs 10.7 for non-Black; high-school completion 26% vs 44%; grade-16/BA-proxy 0.25% vs 0.38%). The actual relationship is a Black DISadvantage that is graded by family socioeconomic status: the attainment gap versus non-Black respondents is largest at LOW family income (~30 percentage points in high-school completion; ~1.5 grade-levels in continuous grade) and narrows toward near-parity at HIGH income (~6 pp; ~0.25 grade-levels). In multivariate models controlling for family income, parental education, baseline cognitive ability (ASVAB), sex and age, the independent Black effect is small and statistically indistinguishable from zero, indicating that the observed Black attainment gap is largely attributable to lower family SES (parental education and income) and lower baseline cognitive scores rather than race per se. The Black×income interaction is directionally consistent with a narrowing gap at higher SES and becomes statistically significant in the imputed OLS (β=0.098, p=0.009). In short: there is no Black advantage; the Black attainment gap is an SES-graded disadvantage that shrinks as socioeconomic status rises.

payload.workflow: 1) Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61, NLSY79); confirmed columns/dtypes: education='Highest grade completed, 1979' (baseline, age 14-22), race='Racial/ethnic cohort, 1979' (1=Black,2=Hispanic,3=NonBlack), SES=1979 family income (1978) + parental education (mother+father grade) + later net wealth. 2) Excluded 2 DK(95) codes and 152 missing education; defined outcomes BA=grade>=16 (n=36, near-empty), HS completion=grade>=12, continuous grade; defined SES level=1979 family income tertiles (Low/Mid/High). 3) Cross-tabbed HS completion, continuous grade, and BA by race x SES tertile and computed the Black gap (NonBlack-Black) within each tier. 4) Logistic regression (HS completion) and OLS (continuous grade) with Black/Hispanic indicators, standardized income, parental-education composite, ASVAB, sex, age, and Black x income interaction (complete-case n=7,521). 5) Robustness: reran models with parental-education composite as the sole SES measure. 6) Imputation sensitivity: median-imputed income and parental education (n=11,037) and reran both models.
